titre: The Calculation That Overstates the Calories in a Handful of Almonds
accroche: The number printed on the label of a bag of almonds is not measured. It comes from a century-old formula that ignores what the body digests.
contenu_vulgarise:
A 28-gram serving of almonds shows about 170 calories on the nutrition label. That number comes from no direct measurement: it results from a calculation, devised in the late 19th century by the American chemist Wilbur O. Atwater, which assigns a fixed energy value to each macronutrient (4 calories per gram of protein, 4 per gram of carbohydrate, 9 per gram of fat), whatever the food that contains them.

## What the Body Never Absorbs

In 2012, a team from the USDA's human nutrition laboratory in Beltsville, Maryland, directly tests this assumption on almonds. Eighteen adults follow, in rotation and for eighteen days each, three controlled diets containing 0, 42, or 84 grams of almonds per day. During the last nine days of each period, the researchers collect all of the participants' urine and feces and precisely measure their energy content. This is the same balance method used to establish the Atwater tables themselves, but applied this time to a whole food rather than to its isolated components, so as to count only the energy actually absorbed by the body.

The result: almonds in fact provide 4.6 calories per gram, versus 6.0 to 6.1 calculated by the Atwater method, that is, 129 calories per 28-gram serving rather than 168 to 170. A gap of 32%. The cause lies in the structure of the almond itself: part of its fat remains locked inside plant cell walls that digestion cannot fully break, and comes out intact, measurable in the feces, without ever having nourished the body.

## A Calorie Is Not Just a Matter of Grams

The gap is no mere anecdote for the Atwater method itself: designed for average food mixtures, it remains broadly reliable for a complete meal, but is systematically wrong for certain foods whose structure holds back part of their energy, beginning with whole tree nuts. Two grams of fat are therefore not always worth the same, depending on the food that encloses them and on how the body manages, or fails, to extract them. Digestion is itself a step in the calculation, not just the composition shown on the package. The same discrepancy is found, to varying degrees, in other whole tree nuts, such as walnuts and pistachios, also studied by the same USDA team.

repere.texte: 4.6 ± 0.8 kcal/g, which is equivalent to 129 kcal/28-g serving [...] significantly less than the energy density of 6.0-6.1 kcal/g as determined by the Atwater factors.
repere.source: Novotny, Gebauer & Baer, “Discrepancy between the Atwater factor predicted and empirically measured energy values of almonds in human diets,” American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2012 (quoted in the original English: 4.6 ± 0.8 kcal/g, or 129 kcal per 28-g serving, versus 6.0-6.1 kcal/g by the Atwater factors)

carte.punch: The label on a bag of almonds measures nothing. It calculates, with a 19th-century formula.
carte.idee: A USDA team measured, in the urine and feces of eighteen volunteers, the energy actually drawn from servings of almonds. Result: 32% fewer calories than the Atwater method predicts, because part of the fat stays locked in cell walls that are never digested.

quiz.question: Why do almonds, in practice, provide fewer calories than the nutrition label predicts?
choix: Because chewing almonds burns more calories than chewing other foods
Because part of their fat stays locked in cell walls that are never fully digested
Because almonds contain less fat than chemical analyses indicate
Because the heat of roasting destroys part of the fats before sale
quiz.explication: Fat present in a food is not necessarily absorbed: in the almond, a fraction remains trapped in intact plant cell walls and comes out in the feces, which the Atwater formula cannot predict.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What energy value does the Atwater method assign to one gram of fat?
choix: 4 calories, as for protein and carbohydrate
9 calories, whatever the food that contains it
4.6 calories, the value measured on almonds
6 calories, the average of the three macronutrients
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Atwater's formula assigns 4 calories per gram to protein and carbohydrate, and 9 to fat, without regard to the food. The 4.6 calories per gram is the measurement obtained on whole almonds: a result, not a factor of the formula.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the USDA team measure the energy actually absorbed?
choix: By weighing the participants every morning for eighteen days
By burning almonds in a calorimeter and reading the heat
By measuring the fats present in the blood after each meal
By collecting all of the participants' urine and feces
quiz_supplementaire.explication: During the last nine days of each period, the researchers collected all the urine and all the feces and measured their energy content. This balance gives the energy absorbed, not merely the energy contained in the food.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what other foods was the same discrepancy found?
choix: In whole grains and dried legumes
In other whole tree nuts, walnuts and pistachios
In whole dairy products, cheeses included
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The same USDA team studied walnuts and pistachios, and finds the discrepancy there to varying degrees. It is the structure of the whole tree nut that holds back part of the energy, not fat content alone.
